articles.title: Circuit mechanisms for disentangled representations and generalization in the hippocampus.
articles.authors: Tang W, Chang H, Liu C, Perez-Hernandez S, Zheng WY, Park J, Karaba LA, Oliva A, Fernandez-Ruiz A.
articles.abstract: Understanding how the heterogeneous activity patterns of individual neurons give rise to coherent population dynamics and cognition is a central challenge in neuroscience. In the hippocampus, neurons are tuned to spatial location, yet their activity is also modulated by multiple external and internal variables and appears to drift randomly over time, making it difficult to link hippocampal computations to behavior. By analyzing hippocampal population dynamics in behaving mice, we reveal a structured organization underlying the diversity of single-neuron responses-the hippocampus encodes different aspects of experience as disentangled variables represented in the co-activity dynamics of cell assemblies. The temporal and contextual components of these representations are governed by local inhibitory interactions and input-driven cell-assembly dynamics, respectively. Our findings reveal the circuit basis of disentangled hippocampal representations, offering a unifying geometric principle of population coding that supports flexible memory representations and enables rapid generalization of prior knowledge to new situations.

articles.title: A Review on the Development and Key Technologies of Embodied Intelligent Industrial Robots in Smart Manufacturing
articles.authors: Jie Wang, Mingsheng Li, Yiming Jiang
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Industrial robots are widely deployed in manufacturing systems to execute repetitive and predefined tasks. However, with the rise of Industry 4.0 and the growing demand for flexible, customized, and human‐centered production, conventional industrial robotic systems increasingly face limitations in adaptability, autonomy, and interaction capability. In this context, embodied intelligent industrial robots (EIIRs) are emerging as a promising paradigm for next‐generation smart manufacturing. Unlike conventional advanced industrial robots, EIIRs are characterized not merely by stronger sensing or more powerful models, but by a closed‐loop intelligence paradigm grounded in body‐environment interaction, feedback‐driven adaptation, and task‐oriented action execution. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the development, defining characteristics, key technologies, representative applications, and future trends of EIIRs in smart manufacturing. First, the conceptual foundations and defining characteristics of EIIRs are clarified, with particular emphasis on physical embodiment, perception‐action coupling, feedback‐driven closed‐loop adaptation, and grounded mapping from semantic goals to physical actions. Second, the key technological architecture of EIIRs is analyzed from the perspectives of embodied perception, embodied decision‐making and task planning, and embodied control and execution, together with a comparative discussion of traditional hierarchical architectures and embodied closed‐loop architectures. Third, the practical value of EIIRs is examined through representative industrial scenarios, including robotic welding, robotic grinding, precision assembly, human–robot collaboration, and multi‐robot cooperation. Finally, the major technical challenges, future evolution path, and critical turning points of EIIRs are discussed, including industrial world models, long‐horizon task execution, sim‐to‐real transfer, real‐time deployment, and safety assurance. This review aims to provide a structured reference for understanding how embodied intelligence can drive the transition of industrial robotics from predefined automation toward grounded, adaptive, and context‐aware task execution in smart manufacturing.

articles.title: Intruding delta waves during REM sleep are associated with tau, amyloid, and forgetting in aging
articles.authors: Tenzin Desel, Matthew P. Walker, Chelsea Brown
articles.abstract: Abstract Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep degrades with age, and more severely in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). REM sleep comprises about twenty percent of adult sleep, alternates between phasic and tonic periods, and includes delta waves (1-4 Hz) in two forms: fast sawtooth waves and slower, NREM-like waves, whose expression dynamically varies across REM periods. Yet, the functional relevance of these REM sleep delta waves remains unknown. Here, using two independent cohorts, we show that aging is associated with a shift from fast sawtooth to slow NREM-like delta waves, particularly during phasic REM sleep - a period typically marked by high cortical activation. Beyond chronological age, this shift is associated with amyloid-β and tau burden, suggesting that AD pathology is associated with REM-specific oscillatory patterns. Furthermore, this shift in REM oscillations is linked to impaired overnight memory consolidation, independent of NREM sleep quality. Moreover, variation in APOE alleles, a major genetic risk factor for AD, was independently associated with a reduction in fast sawtooth wave density, thereby linking a genetic predisposition for AD to these specific REM microstructural changes. These findings identify a signature of memory decline in aging and implicate REM sleep as a distinct vulnerable substrate through which AD pathology may impair brain function.

articles.title: Postnatal development of inhibition associated with entorhinal cortex input to the CA1 hippocampus
articles.authors: Alina Vazetdinova, Ilgam Khalilov, Azat Gainutdinov
articles.abstract: During early development, temporoammonic (TA) input from the entorhinal cortex provides major excitatory drive to the CA1 hippocampus, yet whether this excitation is balanced by feedforward inhibition remains unclear. Using whole-cell recordings from CA1 pyramidal cells (PCs) in intact hippocampi, we found that TA stimulation reliably evoked monosynaptic excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) from birth, whereas inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) were frequently absent or severely delayed during the first postnatal week. The delay between evoked EPSCs and IPSCs shortened with age, narrowing the temporal integration window. Similar dynamics occurred during early sharp waves in vivo, where IPSC bursts followed EPSC bursts by tens of milliseconds, with this delay decreasing over development. Using paired recordings from fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs) and PCs, we identified two mechanisms underlying delayed feedforward inhibition during the first postnatal week: (i) low FS-IN→PC connectivity, and (ii) a weak monosynaptic entorhinal cortex (EC) drive to FS-INs. By the end of the second week, EC inputs to FS-INs surpassed those to PCs. Together, these findings reveal that feedforward inhibition in the EC-CA1 circuit is delayed, creating a broad temporal window for synaptic integration during the neonatal period. We propose that this extended window supports global bursting, with progressive inhibition maturation contributing to the switch toward sparse coding. KEY POINTS: Feedforward inhibition upon entorhinal input is developmentally delayed, creating a broad temporal integration window in the neonatal CA1 hippocampus. Weak entorhinal drive to CA1 fast-spiking interneurons is the primary cause of delayed feedforward inhibition in neonates. Delayed inhibition is a consistent feature of CA1 early sharp waves in vivo. Maturation of feedforward inhibition may drive the switch from global 'bursting' to sparse coding.

articles.title: Robot-assisted ultrasound imaging towards embodied intelligence: a survey
articles.authors: Qin Fang, Jian Chen, Haochuan Tong
articles.abstract: Robot-assisted ultrasound imaging has emerged as an important direction for improving the consistency, accessibility, and safety of ultrasound examinations. Unlike conventional image interpretation tasks, ultrasound image quality is determined by the closed-loop interaction among probe motion, contact force, tissue deformation, acoustic coupling, and clinical intent, making robot-assisted ultrasound imaging a representative scenario for embodied intelligence. In this survey, embodied intelligence refers to the coordination of sensing, actuation, and adaptive decision-making within a physical perception-action loop that links probe manipulation to imaging outcomes. Rather than reviewing artificial intelligence algorithms or robotic platforms in isolation, this paper analyzes how sonographer-like scanning intelligence is progressively externalized into robotic morphology, sensing architectures, control strategies, simulation environments, and learning-based autonomy. We first summarize clinical application scenarios and their task-specific embodied requirements. We then review foundational technologies, including mechanical design, actuation mechanisms, ultrasound and external sensing, and force-position interaction control. We emphasize sensor-actuator integration, contact-force measurement, mechanical compliance, and engineering trade-offs that influence scanning performance. Ultrasound imaging and scanning simulation are discussed as infrastructures for modeling action-dependent image formation and supporting policy learning. Recent advances in reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and methods based on large language models are examined from the perspective of embodied perception-action coupling. Finally, we discuss future challenges in patient-safe embodiment, calibrated multimodal perception, measurable sim-to-real transfer, clinically supervised autonomy, and translational validation.

articles.title: The intermediate hippocampus integrates shock-observation and spatial information during observational fear memory in male rats
articles.authors: Frédéric Michon, Valeria Gazzola, Christian Keysers
articles.abstract: Learning where danger lurks by observing others requires linking another individual’s distress to one’s own representation of space. How the hippocampus implements this mapping is unknown. We recorded Neuropixels activity across the dorsal, intermediate and ventral hippocampus of male rats during contextual fear learning by observation, subsequent rest and recall. Observers showed increased immobility in the context where they had witnessed a conspecific receive footshocks, with substantial inter-individual variability. Pyramidal neurons were recruited by shock observation, with enriched shock-excited cells in the intermediate hippocampus. In the dorsal and intermediate hippocampus, shock-observation responses scaled with baseline place-field firing, revealing a gain-like conjunctive code between observed distress and observer’s position. Following learning, shock-context spatial representations were selectively stabilized in the intermediate hippocampus, and post-learning sharp-wave ripples preferentially reactivated shock-context ensembles, especially in animals expressing contextual freezing. These findings identify candidate hippocampal mechanisms by which socially acquired threat information are mapped onto the observer’s spatial representation and consolidated into memory. The authors find that in rats, responses to witnessing others’ distress scale with hippocampal place-field firing, linking observed danger to the observer’s location. Associated spatial maps are stabilized and reactivated, particularly in the intermediate hippocampus.

articles.title: SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models
articles.authors: Jiaming Hu, Shi Bo, Yan Zheng
articles.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) enable world models to plan from images by predicting future embeddings. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly incorporate task-relevant state information, so the physical state that determines task progress may not be reliably captured in the latent space. Supervising world models with simulator state can make planning more informative, but it requires deciding which state features matter. Features are typically selected by hand or weighted uniformly, and a uniform weighting gives every standardized state feature equal influence, so redundant coordinates can overcount the same variation, while irrelevant ones can obscure task-relevant differences. To address this limitation, we propose SWIM (State Weighting with Inverse-Dynamics Model), which learns state weights from offline trajectories by predicting recorded actions from current states and observed future displacements. The learned weights quantify each feature's contribution to action prediction and define a weighted state metric for state-supervised training, which we demonstrate by aligning latent and state distances. The inverse-dynamics model is used only during training, so the resulting world model plans from images with no additional planning-time computation. Across five simulated robotic manipulation tasks, SWIM consistently improves planning success over uniform state weighting.

articles.title: Reinforcement Learning with World Models in the Era of Scale: From Online Imagination to World Action Models
articles.authors: Wojciech Dąbrowicki, Andrzej Rusiecki
articles.abstract: Abstract In World Model Reinforcement Learning (WM-RL), agents learn a parameterized model of environmental dynamics that serves as the basis for planning, imagination-based policy training, or synthetic data generation in decision making tasks. From 2019 to 2026, a drastic phase transition took place within this field. Initially started as an effort to improve efficiency in visual control tasks, WM-RL has become the core of interdisciplinary AI infrastructure. Today, internet-scale video-based generative world foundation models allow the autonomous vehicle pipeline to learn generalist policies from unlabeled human video, facilitating applications in medical therapy and molecular dynamics. To review the entire trajectory of WM-RL research, it is necessary to synthesize key sources that summarize the advances made throughout the years. Three prominent paradigm shifts are observed during this period. These include the shift from online Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) to pretrain-first imagination-only policy training; architecture integration from decoupled worlds and policies to unified World Action Models; and the generalization of specific algorithms to physical AI infrastructure for all MBRL applications. Regarding architecture, WM-RL follows several generations of innovations. They include PlaNet, Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM), the Dreamer family, value-equivalent implicit models, Transformer-based world models, diffusion dynamics, and the abstract-space Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor. In this review, we examine WM-RL from multiple aspects, ranging from general model-based reinforcement learning, robotic manipulation, navigation, autonomous driving, multi-agent systems, large language model agents, healthcare, and games. The usage of world models varies widely depending on the application areas, while the validated architectures are discussed accordingly.

articles.title: Hippocampal replay repairs the cognitive map for flexible planning
articles.authors: Armin Bazarjani, Caitlin S. Mallory, David Foster
articles.abstract: Hippocampal replay is structured: prospective replay typically precedes retrospective replay, each aligns with the animal's future and past paths, and replay sometimes targets abandoned goals. We propose that replay repairs the cognitive map. A map that supports efficient planning precomputes expected paths; because plans terminate at the goal, the goal is part of the structure it represents. Every goal change therefore leaves the map incorrect and requires two repairs: one for the goal adopted, one for the goal left behind. The larger is expressed first, and the path each takes determines what it depicts, accounting for replay's ordering, direction, and paradoxical content. The model also generates the predictions that this ordering should invert when past and future paths converge. Recordings from rats foraging in an open arena confirm this: replay order is not as fixed as previously believed, but varies with trajectory geometry and the proximity of the abandoned goal.

articles.title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
articles.authors: Tobias Schmidt, Rodrigo González Laiz, Krisztián Szuppinger
articles.abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.

articles.title: PRIME W0: Physical Priors from World Models for Embodied Manipulation
articles.authors: Huabin Peng, Fagang Jin, Yancong Wei
articles.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at instruction following, yet most remain feed-forward: they condition actions only on the current observation and discard both long-horizon temporal context and the hierarchical structure of VLM representations. We present PRIME W0, a hierarchical conditional flow-matching framework that closes this gap through three synergistic designs: (1)per-layer KV injection from a pretrained VLM into an Adaptive MoE action expert; (2)dynamics-aware conditioning via asynchronous world-model subgoal-image prediction and a DINOv2 historical-frame semantic bridge; and (3)Action Dynamic Manifold (ADM) flow matching with covariance-structured noise that respects robot kinematic coupling. PRIME W0 is trained in four stages---VLM pre-training, DAT/NTP visuomotor pre-training, DiT flow-matching decoder assembly with WM injection, and end-to-end SFT---and achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO and real-robot benchmarks, with systematic ablations validating each architectural component.

articles.title: Neuroengineering Approaches in Rett Syndrome: Eye Tracking, Virtual Reality, Brain–Computer Interfaces, and Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation
articles.authors: Rosa Angela Fabio
articles.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) can restrict the motor and verbal responses needed for conventional assessment and rehabilitation. This non-systematic critical narrative review examines human RTT evidence on eye tracking, virtual reality (VR), electroencephalography (EEG), brain–computer interfaces (BCIs), wearable sensing, and non-invasive brain stimulation, with an evidence horizon of 25 August 2026. The searches were non-exhaustive, and the selected evidence inventory does not constitute a systematic census of all eligible studies. In the author’s interpretation of heterogeneous evidence, eye-gaze augmentative and alternative communication has the clearest implementation experience in selected individuals; this does not constitute a comparative efficacy grade. Gaze-adapted assessment requires task-specific validation. Small VR studies provide feasibility and outcome-specific controlled findings, without established durable participation benefits. EEG studies support candidate biomarkers and task-state measurement, rather than demonstrated therapeutic benefit. No peer-reviewed RTT-specific study demonstrating clinical efficacy of real-time EEG command control was located by the stated searches; programme reports, conference material, and registry eligibility are distinguished from such evidence. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) remains a physiological probe, transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) an experimental adjunct supported by limited controlled evidence, and transcranial photobiomodulation a therapeutic hypothesis. A proposed multimodal framework separates documented component uses from unvalidated integration and adaptive links.

articles.title: Evolutionary neuropharmacology of serotonergic psychedelics: a cross-species perspective on mechanisms, consciousness, and therapeutic potential.
articles.authors: Zhai H, Wang H, Wang Y, Wang X.
articles.abstract: Serotonergic psychedelics have revitalized psychiatric research by producing rapid and potentially sustained clinical benefits in selected neuropsychiatric conditions. However, the mechanisms linking receptor activation to neural plasticity, altered conscious experience, and clinical improvement remain incompletely understood, while the evolutionary origins of psychedelic signaling and the translational value of animal models continue to be actively debated. In this review, we integrate evolutionary biology, molecular pharmacology, comparative neuroscience, and computational psychiatry into a unified framework for understanding psychedelic action across biological scales. Building upon predictive processing and the Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) framework, we discuss how serotonergic psychedelics transiently reshape hierarchical inference, providing computational principles that can be experimentally investigated across species despite profound differences in neural architecture and subjective experience. Comparative analyses from invertebrates to non-human primates further suggest that conserved receptor pharmacology coexists with species-specific circuit organization, highlighting that animal models should be interpreted as complementary platforms for investigating molecular, cellular, and computational mechanisms rather than direct proxies for human hallucinatory experiences. We further discuss preclinical and emerging translational evidence suggesting that biased receptor signaling and non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens may partially dissociate plasticity-related therapeutic actions from hallucinogenic effects, providing new opportunities for mechanism-based drug development. By integrating evolutionary biology with molecular psychiatry, this review provides a mechanistic framework linking receptor pharmacology, neural plasticity, circuit computation, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby offering new conceptual and experimental strategies for developing next-generation psychedelic therapeutics.

articles.title: Embodied at Sea: Imitation Learning for Multi-Task Underwater Manipulation
articles.authors: Greta Perez-Haiek, Luca Macesanu, Kevin Angers
articles.abstract: Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Across three tasks on 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts in a pool, 10 models outperformed the baseline, with the highest-performing model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate, including partial successes. Results are also introduced from a case study evaluating the performance of a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and a generalist VLA (SmolVLA) policy for two tasks in marine archaeology and conservation: grasping and mooring. Experiments are performed on an ROV on and around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at Manoel Island Marina, Malta. Across 748 collected episodes and 508 gradable on-hardware rollouts, the ACT policy substantially outperformed SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success rate), earning a 66.7% success rate on the most successful task at the marine archaeological site. To enable further contributions to embodied intelligence in marine field robotics, the BLUEMBODIED KIT used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV has been open sourced.

articles.title: Seeing and Imagining as One: Unified Video Generation and 4D Perception for Embodied World Modeling
articles.authors: Haitang Feng, Zhuoman Liu, Zhennan Wang
articles.abstract: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.

articles.title: EEG Feature-level integration for robust command generation in SSVEP-based brain-computer interfaces.
articles.authors: Yuan X, Zhang L, Zhou A.
articles.abstract: Background Steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP)-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have been widely studied for efficient command generation via spatiotemporal information integration and advanced stimulation paradigms. However, users may intentionally or unintentionally suppress SSVEP responses, leading to the SSVEP Blocking Response (SSVEP-BR). This phenomenon, characterized by attenuation or disappearance of SSVEP, has been largely overlooked despite its potential for command generation without additional stimuli. New method This study aimed to exploit SSVEP-BR to enhance command generation under limited visual stimulation. A novel detection method was proposed based on alpha rhythm sensitivity during transitions between SSVEP and SSVEP-BR states. An EEG feature-level integration strategy was further developed to integrate correlation and alpha rhythm features, enabling effective characterization of their temporal evolution. An asynchronous BCI system was implemented for real-time robotic arm control. Results Experiments on 11 offline subjects demonstrated that the proposed method improved SSVEP-BR detection performance. Compared with the previous SSVEP-BR detection framework, average improvements of 17.11%, 8.50%, and 5.44% were achieved in precision, recall, and specificity, respectively. Furthermore, an online robotic grasping experiment was conducted with 5 subjects, where the proposed asynchronous BCI system achieved 8-command generation using two stimulation frequencies. Comparison with existing methods Unlike prior studies focusing on algorithmic optimization or stimulation design, this work introduced SSVEP-BR as an additional controllable neural response and demonstrated its effectiveness in improving command generation without increasing stimulus complexity. Conclusions Incorporating SSVEP-BR into SSVEP-based BCI frameworks improved flexibility and robustness, enhancing the practicality of asynchronous brain computer interaction systems.

articles.title: Can Smartphones Be Alive? On Artificial Living Entities, Consciousness, and Ethics
articles.authors: Kees van Zon
articles.venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Consciousness
articles.abstract: This paper evaluates smartphones against a previously proposed, theory-relative criterion for artificial aliveness and explores the implications of adopting that criterion. Modern smartphones integrate substantial computational power, rich sensor suites, persistent energy flows, and continuous interaction with their environments. This paper asks whether such devices could, in principle, be engineered to function as artificial living entities. Building on a previously proposed sufficiency condition for aliveness that requires sustained organization far from equilibrium and self-referential regulation of one’s own continued viability, we assess whether a smartphone-based system could meet these criteria. We examine whether the structural and functional characteristics commonly associated with biological organisms can be implemented using current smartphone hardware and software and find that this is largely feasible. We then analyze the additional requirements imposed by self-referential self-maintenance, including internal self-modeling, viability evaluation, embodied causal coupling, and persistence of identity over time. While these capabilities require substantial system-level integration and incremental development, no fundamental scientific or technological obstacles are identified. The paper further considers whether such an entity could be conscious, arguing that self-referential viability regulation alone does not imply consciousness and that the emergence of phenomenology remains unresolved. Finally, we argue that even in the absence of consciousness, such entities would challenge existing distinctions between tools and organisms and raise ethical questions about autonomy, intervention, and termination.

articles.title: Disentangled Multimodal Spatiotemporal Learning for Hybrid EEG-fNIRS Brain-Computer Interface.
articles.authors: Xu Y, Vong CM, Xu Z, Fu J, Li J, Chen C.
articles.abstract: The hybrid EEG-fNIRS Brain-computer interface (BCI) combines the high temporal resolution of electroencephalography (EEG) with the high spatial resolution of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to enable comprehensive brain activity detection. However, integrating these modalities to obtain highly discriminative features remains challenging. Most existing methods fail to effectively capture the spatiotemporal coupling features and correlations between EEG and fNIRS signals. Furthermore, these methods adopt a holistic learning paradigm for the representation of each modality, leading to unrefined and redundant multimodal representations. To address these challenges, we propose a disentangled multimodal spatiotemporal learning (DMSL) method for hybrid EEG-fNIRS BCI systems, which simultaneously performs multimodal spatiotemporal coupling and disentangled representation learning within a unified framework. Specifically, DMSL utilizes a compact convolutional module with one-dimensional temporal and spatial convolution layers to extract complex spatiotemporal patterns from each modality and introduces a multimodal attention interaction module to comprehensively capture the inter-modality correlations, enhancing the representations for each modality. Subsequently, DMSL designs an adaptive multi-branch graph convolutional module based on reconstructed channels to effectively capture the spatiotemporal coupling features, incorporating modality consistency and disparity constraints to disentangle common and modality-specific representations for each modality. These disentangled representations are finally adaptively fused to perform different task predictions. The proposed DMSL demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on publicly available datasets for mental arithmetic, motor imagery, and emotion recognition tasks, exceeding the best baselines by 2.34%, 0.59%, and 1.47%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of DMSL in improving EEG-fNIRS decoding and its strong generalization ability in BCI applications.

articles.title: Prior-Guided Dual Stream Time-Frequency Meta Learning Network for Few-Shot Cross-Domain Fault Diagnosis
articles.authors: Zishan Xie, Jun Cheng, Changcai Yang
articles.abstract: Abstract Drastic fluctuations in fault feature distributions under large-span variable speeds, compounded by target domain label scarcity, severely degrade the generalization performance of diagnostic models. To address these challenges, a Prior-Guided Time-Frequency Dual-Stream Meta-Learning network (PR-TFML) is proposed in this paper. By leveraging the deeply decoupled synergy between mechanistic knowledge and data-driven learning, PR-TFML constructs a multimodal feature extraction architecture composed of complementary time-domain and time-frequency branches. The time-domain branch employs large-receptive-field convolutions to capture nonstationary transient impact characteristics, while the time-frequency branch extracts high-dimensional evolutionary features through an embedded short-time Fourier transform layer. Building upon this, a physical prior mapping branch is introduced to construct a compact hybrid prior by combining macroscopic operating conditions (e.g., rotational speed) with intrinsic statistical and energy-based descriptors (e.g., kurtosis, envelope energy, and wavelet energy). This prior is transformed into domain-invariant semantic anchors, enabling adaptive calibration against distribution shifts. Furthermore, guided by physical priors, an explicit alignment-enhanced meta-optimization strategy couples Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning with Correlation Alignment constraints to facilitate rapid cross-domain adaptation and feature distribution alignment under extreme few-shot conditions. Extensive experiments conducted on the HUST bearing and BJTU WT-Planetary gearbox datasets demonstrate that PR-TFML maintains a high degree of feature consistency and diagnostic robustness under extreme few-shot and large-span variable operating conditions. This method effectively mitigates the feature degradation inherent in purely data-driven models under domain shifts, providing a reliable physics-guided paradigm with strong generalization capability for the cross-domain predictive maintenance of complex rotating machinery.

articles.title: NCEL: Convolution-Enhanced Lightweight Neural Architecture for Robust EEG Signal Decoding in Noninvasive Brain-Computer Interfaces
articles.authors: Yongwei LI, Yongfei Huang, Wenhui Chen
articles.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and clinical neuro-diagnostics due to its non-invasiveness and high temporal resolution. However, robust EEG decoding remains challenging, particularly for resource-constrained deployments. While lightweight architectures like EEGNet offer favorable parameter efficiency, their reliance on fixed convolution kernels and restricted temporal receptive fields inherently limits their performance in complex, highly variable scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a Neural Convolution-Enhanced Lightweight network (NCEL) that augments spatiotemporal EEG representations while preserving structural compactness. Specifically, a dynamic neural convolution module (NCM) is designed to learn input-dependent temporal filtering strategies for trial-to-trial variability and session-related distribution shifts.Furthermore, parallel multiscale temporal convolution branches are integrated to concurrently capture short-term local waveform transients and long-interval rhythmic dependencies. Finally, a lightweight channel-attention gating mechanism adaptively recalibrates intermediate representations, amplifying task-relevant neural responses while suppressing noise-dominated channels. Extensive evaluations on five benchmark datasets (BCIC IV-2a, BCIC IV-2b, ERN, SMR, and P300) demonstrate that NCEL achieves a mean classification accuracy of 82.75\% on BCIC IV-2b. Notably, NCEL achieves higher mean performance than the EEGNet reference values, with performance gains of 12.53 percentage points on the P300 dataset and 9.54 percentage points on BCIC IV-2b, while maintaining only $\sim$0.008M parameters. Additional subject-specific session-disjoint evaluations show comparable cross-session performance to EEGNet on BCIC IV-2a and a 1.80-percentage-point mean improvement on BCIC IV-2b. Overall, NCEL provides a parameter-efficient framework for resource-constrained EEG decoding, while broader cross-session generalization requires further validation.

articles.title: Emergence of Goal-Directed Behaviors via Active Inference With Self-Prior.
articles.authors: Kim D, Kanazawa H, Yoshida N, Kuniyoshi Y.
articles.abstract: Infants often exhibit goal-directed behaviors, such as reaching for a sensory stimulus, even when no external reward criterion is provided. These intrinsically motivated behaviors facilitate spontaneous exploration and learning of the body and environment during early developmental stages. Although computational modeling can offer insight into the mechanisms underlying such behaviors, many existing studies on intrinsic motivation focus primarily on how exploration contributes to acquiring external rewards. In this paper, we propose a novel density model for an agent's own multimodal sensory experiences, called the "self-prior," and investigate whether it can autonomously induce goal-directed behavior. Integrated within an active inference framework based on the free energy principle, the self-prior generates behavioral references purely from an intrinsic process that minimizes mismatches between average past sensory experiences and current observations. This mechanism is also analogous to the acquisition and utilization of a body schema through continuous interaction with the environment. We examine this approach in a simulated environment and confirm that the agent spontaneously reaches toward a tactile stimulus. Our study implements intrinsically motivated behavior shaped by the agent's own sensory experiences, demonstrating the spontaneous emergence of intentional behavior during early development. SUMMARY: Suggests a computational model for early intentional behavior, integrating body-schema formation and goal-directed actions under the free energy principle. Introduces a self-prior as an internal density model that drives the emergence of goal-directed behaviors without external rewards. Demonstrates spontaneous reaching for a sticker by minimizing mismatches between observed multimodal sensory inputs and the empirically acquired self-prior.

articles.title: Mental Scene and Memory Construction and the Hippocampus.
articles.authors: Rolls ET.
articles.abstract: A neurocomputational theory of scene and memory construction during memory recall, prospective thinking, and autobiographical memory is described. The theory describes the nature of the representation of scenes using spatial view cells in a continuous attractor network in the medial parahippocampal cortex, and how the location in the scene being represented can be shifted by self-motion eye position update even when the scene is not visible. The theory builds on the evidence for humans for a ventromedial visual cortical scene pathway via the prostriate cortex and ventromedial visual cortical regions to the medial parahippocampal scene (or place) area where scenes are represented. The approach builds on a theory about how visual features in scenes are used along this pathway to build a continuous attractor network representation of scenes in the medial parahippocampal cortex that represents the relative spatial locations of features or landmarks in the scene. The theory shows how episodic memory can be built in an attractor network in hippocampal CA3 that learns associations between the location in a scene ("where"), the object or person at that location in the scene ("what"), and the reward/affective value conveyed to the hippocampus from the orbitofrontal cortex in part via the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex. The theory of scene construction then shows how backprojections from hippocampal CA1 via the entorhinal cortex to the medial parahippocampal cortex can recall or construct the scene representation in the medial parahippocampal cortex, the parahippocampal scene (or place) area; and how whole memories including visual imagery of objects, rewards, and their locations in scenes can be constructed by iterative neocortical-hippocampal-neocortical processing.

articles.title: Detecting SQL and NoSQL injection in HTTP request payloads using BERT-based models: A unified detection framework with continual learning
articles.authors: Nuntanut Bhooanusas, Araya Srisakulmekee, Ornadda Iamsudha
articles.abstract: SQL injection (SQLi) and NoSQL injection (NoSQLi) remain major security threats to modern web applications. Existing studies commonly focus on a single attack type or analyze database queries rather than HTTP request payloads, while adaptation across SQLi and NoSQLi detection tasks remains underexplored. This paper proposes a unified BERT-based framework for detecting SQLi and NoSQLi directly from HTTP request payloads. Five pre-trained BERT models, representing general-purpose, cybersecurity-oriented, and code-oriented language models, are compared with conventional TF-IDF-based machine learning classifiers under three learning strategies: task-specific learning, sequential continual learning, and joint SQLi–NoSQLi training. The sequential experiments consider both SQLi-to-NoSQLi and NoSQLi-to-SQLi task orders to evaluate knowledge retention and catastrophic forgetting. Experimental results show that task-specific learning generally provides strong domain-specific detection, whereas sequential continual learning enables cross-domain learning but introduces task-order-dependent forgetting in several configurations. Joint training provides more balanced unified detection and avoids task-order dependency, although at a higher training cost. Pattern-level analysis further reveals that strong aggregate performance can coexist with weaknesses for specific injection mechanisms. Overall, the results demonstrate that no learning strategy is universally superior. Rather, task-specific, sequential, and joint learning provide different trade-offs among domain specialization, adaptation, knowledge retention, unified detection, and computational cost.

articles.title: Vision-Language-Action Intelligence for Traditional Industrial Robotic Arms
articles.authors: Weijian Wan
articles.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) intelligence provides a unified route for connecting visual perception, language understanding, and executable control in traditional industrial robotic arms. This paper examines the transition from modular perception-planning-control pipelines to generalist policies that predict robot actions from multimodal observations and instructions. It reviews representative architectures, including RT-1, RT-2, Octo, and OpenVLA, and compares three major action-representation strategies: discrete action tokens, continuous action prediction, and specialised policy heads. Particular attention is given to the role of large-scale robot datasets, vision-language pre-training, action tokenization, and embodiment-specific adaptation. The analysis further considers the progression from multimodal intelligence to embodied intelligence and distinguishes cross-task, cross-environment, and cross-embodiment generalization. Existing results indicate that shared backbones and heterogeneous trajectory data can reduce the cost of adapting policies to new tasks and robot platforms, but reliable industrial deployment still depends on control precision, inference latency, safety constraints, data consistency, and closed-loop feedback. The paper concludes that practical VLA systems for industrial arms will require coordinated advances in data standards, model efficiency, controller integration, and hardware-aware evaluation.
